item.title: Socket Finds Malicious Firefox Extensions as NIST and White House Address AI-Driven Threats
item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 18:00 → 20 Aug 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

Health-ISAC Hacking Healthcare 8-13-2026 — Should Read

NIST is seeking public input on how to modernize the National Vulnerability Database as AI increases the speed, volume, and complexity of vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Feedback is due by October 13, 2026.

  • Health-ISAC reports that NIST has published a request for information on potential changes to the National Vulnerability Database in response to AI-driven changes in the cyber threat landscape.
  • The article describes the NVD as the U.S. government repository of standards-based vulnerability management data and a foundational resource for software security, compliance automation, and cybersecurity risk analysis across public and private sectors.
  • NIST says traditional vulnerability management approaches such as periodic scanning, static prioritization, and manual remediation are increasingly inadequate as AI affects vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
  • The RFI seeks feedback on areas including strategic planning, technical architecture decisions, standards and best practices development, data governance approaches, and community collaborations.
  • Responses to the NIST RFI are due on or before October 13, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Technologies: database

Products: national-vulnerability-database

Vendors: nist

Socket Now Protects the Firefox Extension Ecosystem — May Read

Socket is adding Firefox extension coverage to its browser extension security product, scanning Mozilla’s add-ons ecosystem for malicious behavior, risky permissions, suspicious infrastructure, and dangerous version changes. The launch follows Socket research showing trusted Firefox extensions can be repurposed through automatic updates into wallet stealers, credential thieves, and clipboard monitors.

  • Socket is expanding its browser extension security coverage to Firefox and is proactively scanning every Firefox extension listed in Mozilla's official addons.mozilla.org directory.
  • Mozilla's public API listed 97,100 Firefox-compatible extensions at the time of publication, and Socket says it will continue monitoring new releases for behavior changes.
  • Socket's Firefox threat research identified 77 linked Firefox extension identities active from at least March through August 2026, with 40 confirmed as malicious and 37 described as deceptive sports-score shells connected through shared code, infrastructure, and version histories.
  • The malicious Firefox extensions delivered remotely controlled wallet-phishing pages, captured recovery phrases and private keys, exfiltrated wallet keyrings, or stole credentials and clipboard contents.
  • Firefox extension protection is now available in Experimental to Socket enterprise customers, expanding the browser extension coverage Socket introduced with Chrome.

Technologies: browser

Products: socket, firefox, addons-mozilla-org, webextensions, chrome

Vendors: socket, mozilla

The Smash-and-Grab Era — Optional

Bishop Fox argues that LLMs let attackers run faster, parallel “smash-and-grab” operations that outpace healthcare’s traditional one-threat-at-a-time detection and response model. The key takeaway is that healthcare security teams need to adapt defenses for AI-accelerated attack timelines.

  • The article says the attacker’s goal has not changed in decades, but the amount of time and noise attackers are willing to spend has changed.
  • Bishop Fox CEO Vinnie Liu explains that LLMs collapse attack timelines into parallel attacks.
  • The article says healthcare’s one-threat-at-a-time detection model cannot keep up with these parallel attacks.
  • Bishop Fox is identified as a Health-ISAC Community Services Champion.
  • The article links readers to a Bishop Fox blog titled “The Smash-and-Grab Era.”

Vendors: bishop-fox

Is Cyber missing the Marque? — Optional

A new White House memorandum would let private cybersecurity companies conduct government-authorized offensive cyber operations against transnational cybercriminals outside the U.S., raising major operational, legal, and diplomatic questions. The author argues the key issue is not whether this can disrupt cybercrime, but whether the consequences have been fully considered.

  • The White House issued a presidential memorandum titled “Expanding Capabilities to Combat Transnational Cyber-Enabled Crime.”
  • The memorandum directs the DOJ and DHS to create a program allowing private companies to conduct cyber surveillance and cyber effects operations against transnational criminal organizations outside the United States under U.S. government direction and delegated authority.
  • The author emphasizes that the memorandum is not “hack back,” but says it creates a mechanism for private companies to participate directly in government-authorized offensive cyber operations.
  • The memorandum gives DOJ and DHS 60 days to establish operating procedures, and no operation can be approved until those procedures are in place.
  • Talos reported on UAT-10147, a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group that uses agentic AI in post-compromise operations and deploys the SPECTRE implant with Linux rootkit and BYOVD capabilities.

item.title: Rust Crates Compromise, Siemens S7 Targeting, and Apple Spyware Alerts
item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 14:00 → 20 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Frequently asked questions about the active threat to Siemens S7 Series PLCs — Must Read

U.S. agencies warn that threat actors are using AI-generated scripts to target internet-exposed Siemens S7 PLCs in critical infrastructure, enabling reconnaissance and potential pre-positioning for disruptive attacks. There is no single patch; operators should remove PLCs from internet exposure, segment OT networks, harden access controls, and monitor for suspicious S7comm and snap7 activity.

  • A joint advisory from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA warns that threat actors are actively targeting internet-exposed or insufficiently segmented Siemens S7 Series PLCs across multiple critical infrastructure sectors.
  • The activity affects Siemens S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 PLCs, with the heaviest impact noted in Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Commercial Facilities sectors.
  • The advisory says the attackers are using AI-generated exploitation scripts disguised as legitimate OT monitoring tools to conduct reconnaissance and build capability against exposed PLCs.
  • The advisory does not name any specific CVEs or zero-day vulnerabilities, instead describing exploitation of known weaknesses, weak or default credentials, improper segmentation and unnecessary internet exposure.
  • Recommended mitigations include inventorying Siemens S7 PLCs, applying firmware and engineering software updates, blocking TCP port 102 at the perimeter, restricting engineering software access, enabling stronger access controls, and deploying ICS-aware monitoring and logging.

Technologies: plc, ics-scada

Products: siemens-s7-200, siemens-s7-300, siemens-s7-400, siemens-s7-1200, siemens-s7-1500, tia-portal, step-7, snap7, python-snap7

Vendors: siemens

Popular Rust Crates Compromised in Build-Time Supply Chain Attack — Must Read

Legitimate Rust crates were compromised to add a malicious proc-macro1 dependency that executed malware automatically during Cargo builds across Linux, macOS, and Windows. Any system that built the affected versions should be treated as potentially compromised, checked for the listed IOCs, and have exposed credentials rotated.

  • Socket analyzed a coordinated supply chain attack affecting the legitimate Rust crates arrayref@0.3.10, internment@0.8.7, and append-only-vec@0.1.9.
  • Each malicious release added a dependency on proc-macro1, a threat actor-controlled typosquat of proc-macro2 whose build.rs executed automatically during Cargo builds.
  • The proc-macro1 loader detected the victim operating system and architecture, downloaded a platform-specific payload from 23.254.165.112:9089, and executed it with 23.254.165.112:443 as the command-and-control endpoint.
  • Recovered stage-2 payloads for Linux x86-64, Windows x86-64, and macOS ARM64 shared the same protocol, configuration structure, command set, and cryptographic key material.
  • The Rust Security Response Team removed the affected releases, locked the maintainer account as a precaution, and stated it suspects the maintainer’s computer or crates.io publishing credentials were compromised.

Technologies: package-registry, ci-cd

Products: socket-ai-scanner, rust, cargo, crates-io, arrayref, internment, append-only-vec, proc-macro1, proc-macro2, proc-macro-en, aovine, arone, aronenao, tinymember, tiny-skia

Vendors: socket, rust-project, rustsec, david-roundy, nextron-systems

If Apple says your iPhone was targeted by mercenary spyware, treat it like an incident — Should Read

An Apple Threat Notification should be treated as a serious security incident: verify it independently, preserve evidence, get expert mobile forensic help, then enable Lockdown Mode, update iOS, and harden related accounts. For high-risk users, Lockdown Mode plus continuous mobile monitoring provides the best layered defense against mercenary spyware.

  • Apple published updated guidance on August 13, 2026 explaining its Threat Notification program, while reports documented a new wave of alerts reaching users in 110 countries.
  • Apple says a Threat Notification is a high-confidence alert that a specific person has been individually targeted by mercenary spyware, but it does not confirm that the attack succeeded or that data was stolen.
  • A genuine Apple Threat Notification appears on the Lock Screen and in Settings, arrives by email from threat-notifications@email.apple.com, and can be verified by signing in independently at account.apple.com.
  • The article recommends that recipients verify the alert, seek expert help, preserve evidence before restarting or updating the device, perform forensic collection where possible, enable Lockdown Mode, update iOS, and harden account security.
  • The article says Lockdown Mode reduces the attack surface for high-risk users and that Jamf Mobile Forensics can help enterprise responders analyze iOS devices for signs of mercenary spyware without jailbreaking the device or exposing personal content.

Technologies: mobile-os, identity-provider, mfa

Products: iphone, ios, apple-threat-notifications, lockdown-mode, jamf-mobile-forensics, jamf-for-mobile, pegasus, predator, developer-mode, apple-account

Vendors: apple, jamf, nso-group

item.title: UAT-10147 SPECTRE, Defender BTR.sys abuse, and Rust crate compromise
item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 10:00 → 20 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Two popular Rust crates arrayref and append-only-vec compromised in Supply Chain Attack — Must Read

Two widely used Rust crates, arrayref and append-only-vec, were compromised to add a malicious build-time dependency that downloads and executes a remote payload when projects are compiled. Because arrayref has hundreds of millions of downloads, the incident represents a major Rust supply-chain compromise with broad potential impact.

  • Aikido detected that the Rust crates append-only-vec and arrayref were compromised by adding a dependency on the malicious package proc-macro1.
  • The proc-macro1 package downloads a remote payload during the build process and executes it on the developer’s machine, so compiling a project that pulls in either compromised crate can trigger infection.
  • The malicious build script targets Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64, macOS x86_64, and macOS aarch64 systems.
  • The affected package versions listed in the article are proc-macro-en 1.0.10, proc-macro1 1.0.107, append-only-vec 0.1.9, and arrayref 0.3.10.
  • The article lists 23.254.165.112:9089 as the payload delivery host and 23.254.165.112:443 as the command-and-control host passed to the executed payload.

Technologies: package-registry

Products: append-only-vec, arrayref, proc-macro1, proc-macro-en, proc-macro2, cargo, crates-io, aikido-safe-chain, aikido-intel, aikido-device-protection

Vendors: aikido, rust-project

UAT-10147: Chinese-speaking adversary integrates agentic AI into post-compromise operations — Must Read

Cisco Talos found that the Chinese-speaking cybercrime group UAT-10147 is using agentic AI tools to scale real intrusions against vulnerable Windows and Linux web servers, automating exploitation, reconnaissance, payload deployment, validation, persistence, and troubleshooting. The campaign shows how AI can lower the skill and time needed for complex post-compromise operations while increasing attack volume and efficiency.

  • Cisco Talos identified UAT-10147, a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group, targeting vulnerable Windows and Linux web servers globally across government, education, media, technology, and gaming sectors.
  • Talos found a target list on the actor’s command-and-control server containing approximately 170,000 URLs, which the actor split into 17 files of about 10,000 URLs each.
  • UAT-10147 used publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and offensive tools including Metasploit, ysoserial, PentestGPT, DeepAudit, and multiple privilege escalation exploits in its intrusion operations.
  • On Windows systems, the actor used scripts to download tools and payloads, add IIS directories to Windows Defender exclusions, deploy backdoors such as QuasarRAT, and establish persistence through scheduled tasks or rogue user accounts.
  • Talos assessed that UAT-10147’s use of AI-generated exploitation guidance, automation, validation workflows, and operational documentation helps scale complex attacks while reducing the expertise traditionally required for advanced post-compromise operations.

Technologies: operating-system, web-server, antivirus, ids-ips

Products: windows, linux-kernel, iis, microsoft-defender, powershell, asp-net, dotnet, zimbra-collaboration-suite, apache-nacos, telerik-ui-for-asp-net-ajax, metasploit-framework, ysoserial, pentestgpt, deepaudit, efspotato, quasarrat, meterpreter, snort, clamav

Vendors: cisco, microsoft, linux-kernel-project, zimbra, apache-software-foundation, progress, rapid7, sudo-project, frohoff

BTR Reforged: Weaponizing Defender’s Remediation Driver as a Kernel Operation Primitive — Should Read

Researchers found that Microsoft Defender’s signed Boot-Time Removal driver, BTR.sys, can be repurposed by an attacker with driver-loading privileges to perform kernel-level file and registry operations without exploiting a bug. The key takeaway is that trusted security components can become powerful living-off-the-land primitives, so defenders need behavioral detection around driver loading, ADS configuration, and unusual system-level changes.

  • Check Point Research reverse engineered Microsoft Defender’s Boot-Time Removal driver, BTR.sys, and found that its encrypted transaction format can be constructed to make the signed driver perform file and registry operations from kernel mode.
  • The driver reads an RC4-encrypted configuration blob from an Alternate Data Stream named :changelist, validates structures with a modified CRC-32 scheme, and supports actions including file deletion, directory deletion, file move, registry key deletion, registry value deletion, and registry value creation or modification.
  • The researchers built BTR_CLI, a proof-of-concept tool that extracts BTR.sys from MpEngine.dll, creates valid encrypted transactions, stages the driver as a service, and can trigger execution immediately or at boot.
  • The article demonstrates that staging BTR.sys as a Start=1 driver in the Boot Bus Extender group can run it during an early boot window before Defender’s main user-mode service starts, enabling deletion of Defender components and bypassing Tamper Protection in the tests described.
  • The article states that Microsoft MSRC did not classify the findings for immediate servicing because the technique requires existing administrative privileges, and recommends detection based on behavior such as ADS creation, unusual driver loading, service registry staging, and System-process file deletion.

Technologies: operating-system, antivirus, edr

Products: btr.sys, btr-cli, microsoft-defender, mpengine.dll, windows, sysmon, process-monitor, wdfilter.sys, msmpeng.exe

Vendors: microsoft, check-point-research

Perfect Authentication, Borrowed From a Real Mailbox — Should Read

A phishing email passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC because it was sent from a genuinely compromised utility company mailbox, showing that perfect authentication does not mean a message is safe. The lure used a fake “attached document” link to an unrelated domain with a human-verification gate that blocked automated scanners.

  • Two mailboxes at a multi-site services organization received an “EFT payment summary” email in mid-July 2026 that passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC validation.
  • The message was sent from a real employee mailbox at a real utility company through that company’s Microsoft 365 tenant, indicating the sender account was likely taken over rather than spoofed.
  • The email claimed a payment summary was attached, but no attachment existed, and its only link used the display text “REVIEW ATTACHED DOCUMENT HERE” while pointing to the unrelated domain engastando[.]us.
  • A fresh screenshot of the destination showed a human-verification interstitial with content delivery network branding and no visible username, password, or login form.
  • The landing domain was created in early April 2026, exactly 100 days before the email was sent, and the platform labeled the message as credential theft with 90 percent confidence.

Technologies: email-security, cloud-platform

Products: adaptive-ai, ironscales-platform, microsoft-365

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft, google

item.title: Netskope Survey Highlights AI Governance Risks in Financial Services
item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 02:00 → 20 Aug 06:00 UTC (4 hours)

Balancing AI Speed and Security in Financial Services — Optional

Financial services firms are rapidly adopting AI, but legacy infrastructure, shadow AI, data sprawl, and weak visibility are making governance and security lag behind. The key takeaway is that AI adoption needs integrated zero-trust visibility and controls so security can enable innovation without slowing it down.

  • Netskope surveyed 100 North American IT leaders in financial services and found that 62% of organizations have adopted managed third-party AI applications, 54% are building private internal AI applications, and 26% are experimenting with autonomous AI agents.
  • Only 1 in 100 surveyed organizations believe they can accelerate AI adoption without compromising security or operational integrity.
  • The top concerns identified in the research are shadow AI at 56%, loss of visibility into how AI makes decisions at 53%, and data sprawl and compliance risk at 43%.
  • Legacy architecture is cited by 60% of leaders as the main roadblock to new AI product launches, while 31% cite insufficient investment and 21% point to fragmented, siloed security tools.
  • The article argues that organizations should integrate AI governance into their existing security stack using a zero trust approach rather than relying on standalone AI monitoring tools.

Technologies: casb, dlp, proxy

Products: netskope-platform, netskope-one-ai-guardrails, zero-trust-engine

Vendors: netskope

How Peer2Profit and Astroproxy Turn Your Bandwidth Into Someone Else's Product — Should Read

Silent Push found that Peer2Profit users’ bandwidth is actively resold through Astroproxy, turning ordinary residential, mobile, and corporate IPs into hard-to-detect proxy exit nodes. The biggest risk is that these “not malware” bandwidth-sharing apps can expose internal network resources and damage an organization’s reputation without triggering typical security alerts.

  • Silent Push confirmed an active operational relationship between Peer2Profit and Astroproxy by enrolling a clean residential IP address in Peer2Profit and later observing it tagged in Astroproxy’s residential proxy pool.
  • Peer2Profit recruits users to share bandwidth for payments, while Astroproxy resells that bandwidth commercially at much higher prices, including $7.60 per GB for residential traffic compared with $0.28 per GB paid to users.
  • During a 72-hour enumeration period, Silent Push observed 117,224 unique IPs across Astroproxy’s residential, mobile, and datacenter pools, with the residential pool averaging 1,071 new IPs per hour.
  • The Peer2Profit Windows SDK registers devices with an API, connects to backconnect servers, and relays proxy traffic through a custom protocol using nibble inversion as a simple obfuscation layer.
  • Silent Push found that Astroproxy blocked direct requests to internal IP ranges but could be bypassed with a DNS entry resolving to an internal IP address, allowing access to a residential router management interface through an enrolled proxy node.

Technologies: proxy, router

  • CVE-2026-60702 is a critical Oracle WebLogic Server Core vulnerability that allows a low-privileged attacker with network access over T3 or IIOP to compromise the server.

BOFScale: A CDN-Fronted Tailnet from a BOF-PE — May Read

NetSPI’s BOFScale demonstrates a fully in-memory Tailscale/Headscale tailnet for red-team C2, running inside an implant with no driver, service, disk state, or child processes while tunneling DERP and control traffic as CDN-friendly WebSockets. The key defensive takeaway is to hunt for unexpected processes making WebSocket connections using Tailscale DERP or TS2021 subprotocols, in-memory BOFScale signatures, and unusual local SOCKS5 listeners.

  • BOFScale consists of three tools: a modified in-process Tailscale daemon called tailscaled, a C++ BOF-PE client called tailscale, and socksportfwd for forwarding local ports through the daemon’s SOCKS5 server.
  • The modified Tailscale implementation adds RFC 6455 WebSocket support for both DERP relay traffic and the TS2021 control channel so Headscale and DERP can sit behind CloudFront or Fastly.
  • The tailscaled BOF-PE runs in userspace networking mode with memory-only state, no TUN driver, no Windows service, no disk state, and no child processes after startup.
  • The Headscale Docker Compose stack uses Headscale’s embedded DERP relay, disables Logtail, keeps DERP traffic within the operator-controlled stack, and configures ephemeral implant nodes to be removed after ten minutes offline.
  • The article provides defensive guidance including YARA rules for BOFScale components, hunting for WebSocket upgrades with derp or ts2021 subprotocols, and checking for a SOCKS5 listener bound to 0.0.0.0:1080.

  • AWSHound is a free, self-hosted, read-only collector that turns an AWS account or AWS Organization into a BloodHound Community Edition OpenGraph dataset.
  • Before creating graph edges, AWSHound runs offline IAM policy evaluation so edges exist only when effective permissions resolve to Allow after SCPs, RCPs, permissions boundaries, and relevant resource policies are considered.
  • AWSHound has separate collect, process, emit, and ingest phases, with collection using only read actions such as List, Get, and Describe and emit producing a compressed graph.zip file for BloodHound ingestion.
  • The tool models AWS principals and resources as nodes and capabilities as edges, with only 36 of its 156 edge kinds marked as traversable for BloodHound pathfinding.
  • AWSHound currently includes collectors for IAM, Organizations, S3, KMS, SSM, EC2, Lambda, CloudFormation, and EKS, with future collectors planned for Bedrock, ECR, ECS, and CodeBuild.

AWSHound: An OpenSource AWS OpenGraph Collector — May Read

AWSHound is a new open-source, read-only collector that turns AWS accounts or entire Organizations into BloodHound OpenGraph data so teams can find real AWS attack paths after evaluating IAM policies, SCPs, resource policies, boundaries, and conditions offline. Its key value is showing how individually boring AWS permissions can combine into practical privilege-escalation and cross-account compromise paths.

  • AWSHound is a free, self-hosted, read-only collector that turns an AWS account or AWS Organization into a BloodHound Community Edition OpenGraph dataset.
  • Before creating graph edges, AWSHound runs offline IAM policy evaluation so edges exist only when effective permissions resolve to Allow after SCPs, RCPs, permissions boundaries, and relevant resource policies are considered.
  • AWSHound has separate collect, process, emit, and ingest phases, with collection using only read actions such as List, Get, and Describe and emit producing a compressed graph.zip file for BloodHound ingestion.
  • The tool models AWS principals and resources as nodes and capabilities as edges, with only 36 of its 156 edge kinds marked as traversable for BloodHound pathfinding.
  • AWSHound currently includes collectors for IAM, Organizations, S3, KMS, SSM, EC2, Lambda, CloudFormation, and EKS, with future collectors planned for Bedrock, ECR, ECS, and CodeBuild.
